Optimistic Task Inference for Behavior
Foundation Models

Thomas Rupf Affiliation: ETH Zürich, Switzerland Email: thrupf@ethz.ch    Marco Bagatella    Marin Vlastelica Affiliation: ETH Zürich, Switzerland    Andreas Krause Affiliation: ETH Zürich, Switzerland Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, Germany
Abstract

Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) are capable of retrieving high-performing policy for any reward function specified directly at test-time, commonly referred to as zero-shot reinforcement learning (RL). While this is a very efficient process in terms of compute, it can be less so in terms of data: as a standard assumption, BFMs require computing rewards over a non-negligible inference dataset, assuming either access to a functional form of rewards, or significant labeling efforts. To alleviate these limitations, we tackle the problem of task inference purely through interaction with the environment at test-time. We propose OpTI-BFM, an optimistic decision criterion that directly models uncertainty over reward functions and guides BFMs in data collection for task inference. Formally, we provide a regret bound for well-trained BFMs through a direct connection to upper-confidence algorithms for linear bandits. Empirically, we evaluate OpTI-BFM on established zero-shot benchmarks, and observe that it enables successor-features-based BFMs to identify and optimize an unseen reward function in a handful of episodes with minimal compute overhead. Code is available at https://github.com/ThomasRupf/opti-bfm.

1 Introduction

Zero-shot reinforcement learning (Touati et al., 2023) has gradually gained relevance as a powerful generalization of standard, single-reward RL (Sutton & Barto, 2018; Silver et al., 2021). Zero-shot agents are designed to distill optimal policies for a set of reward functions from unlabeled, offline data (Touati & Ollivier, 2021; Agarwal et al., 2024; Park et al., 2024; Jajoo et al., 2025). As these methods scale to more complex and broader environments, they are often referred to as Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) (Park et al., 2024; Tirinzoni et al., 2025). At their core, the majority of BFMs rely on Universal Successor Features (Ma et al. (2020), USFs). These methods build upon explicit representations of states (features): given a set of policies, the expected discounted sum of features along each policy’s trajectory may be estimated completely offline (e.g., through TD learning) (Dayan, 1993; Barreto et al., 2017). As long as a reward function lies within the span of features, zero-shot policy evaluation can be performed through a simple scalar product, which in turn enables zero-shot policy improvement, i.e., each policy is implicitly paired with a reward function and updated towards optimality (Touati & Ollivier, 2021).

Once this unsupervised pre-training phase is complete, USFs yield a set of learned policies. Given a reward function that is linear in the features, its optimal policy is by construction indexed by the linear weights describing the reward function in the basis of features, which can in turn be interpreted as task embeddings. The process of finding the optimal policy, which we refer to as task inference, thus corresponds to solving a linear regression problem. While this process is remarkably efficient in terms of compute, it retains strict requirements in terms of data: a dataset of labeled (state, reward) pairs needs to be provided. In simple settings, this necessity is not particularly problematic: BFMs have been largely trained in simulations (Touati et al., 2023; Park et al., 2024; Tirinzoni et al., 2025), which makes generating reward labels for the pre-training dataset, or additional data, particularly convenient. Realistically, however, (i) the pre-training dataset might be unavailable or proprietary and, most importantly, (ii) labeling states with rewards might incur significant costs. For instance, when BFMs are pre-trained directly from pixels, evaluating success from a single image is not a straightforward or cheap operation.

In order to alleviate these issues, we explore an alternative framework for task inference, which instead aims to collect a small amount of data directly during deployment (see Figure 1). This removes the need to access the pre-training dataset (i) and may require fewer labels (ii), as the data can be collected actively. To navigate this setting, we propose OpTI-BFM, a decision criterion that curates a sequence of task embeddings. Starting from an uninformed prior, OpTI-BFM leverages the linear relationship between features and rewards to update its belief over the space of rewards. A BFM conditioned on meaningfully chosen task embeddings can then interact with the environment for a few steps: labeling the states that are visited allows accurate task estimation with minimal labeling efforts. Crucially, if the underlying BFM is well-trained, we show that control reduces to a bandit problem over tasks. Under this assumption, we can provide regret guarantees for OpTI-BFM. When considering established zero-shot benchmarks in the Deepmind Control Suite (DMC) (Tassa et al., 2018), we find that OpTI-BFM requires only a handful of episodes to correctly identify the task, eventually matching or surpassing the performance that the standard offline reward inference pipeline achieves with significantly more data.

2 Preliminaries

Notation

We model the environment as a reward-free Markov Decision Process (MDP) ℳ=(S,A,P,μ,γ)\mathcal{M}=(S,A,P,\mu,\gamma) where SS and AA are state and action spaces, respectively, P⁡(d​s′|s,a)P(ds^{\prime}|s,a) is a probability measure describing the likelihood of transitions, μ⁡(d​s)\mu(ds) is a measure describing the initial state distribution, and γ\gamma is a discount factor. Given a policy π:S→Δ⁡(A)\pi:S\to\Delta(A) and a state-action pair (s0,a0)∈S×A(s_{0},a_{0})\in S\times A we use 𝔼[⋅|s0,a0,π]\mathbb{E}\left[{\cdot}\ \middle|\ {s_{0},a_{0},\pi}\right] to denote expectations w.r.t. state-action sequences ((st,at))t≥0((s_{t},a_{t}))_{t\geq 0} defined by sampling at∼π⁡(st)a_{t}\sim\pi(s_{t}) and st+1∼P⁡(st,at)s_{t+1}\sim P(s_{t},a_{t}). For a given reward function r:S→ℝr:S\to\mathbb{R}, we define the policy’s state-action value function as the discounted sum of future rewards Qrπ(s0,a0)=∑t≥0γt𝔼[r(st)|s0,a0,π]Q_{r}^{\pi}(s_{0},a_{0})=\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\mathbb{E}\left[{r(s_{t})}\ \middle|\ {s_{0},a_{0},\pi}\right].

Successor Features and Behavior Foundation Models

For a specific feature map ϕ:S→ℝd\phi:S\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, Successor Features (Barreto et al. (2017), SFs) generalize state-action value functions by modeling the expected discounted sum of features under a policy π\pi:

ψπ(s0,a0)=∑t≥0γt𝔼[ϕ(st)|s0,a0,π].\displaystyle\psi^{\pi}(s_{0},a_{0})=\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\,\mathbb{E}\left[{\phi(s_{t})}\ \middle|\ {s_{0},a_{0},\pi}\right]. (1)

SFs allow zero-shot policy evaluation for any reward that lies in the span of the features: if r⁡(s)=z⊤​ϕ​(s)r(s)=z^{\top}\phi(s) for some z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the Q-function is a linear function of SFs:

Qrπ(s0,a0)=∑t≥0γt𝔼[r(st)|s0,a0,π]=∑t≥0γt𝔼[z⊤ϕ(st)|s0,a0,π]=z⊤ψπ(s0,a0)\displaystyle Q_{r}^{\pi}(s_{0},a_{0})=\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\,\mathbb{E}\left[{r(s_{t})}\ \middle|\ {s_{0},a_{0},\pi}\right]=\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\,\mathbb{E}\left[{z^{\top}\phi(s_{t})}\ \middle|\ {s_{0},a_{0},\pi}\right]=z^{\top}\psi^{\pi}(s_{0},a_{0}) (2)

A similar structure also holds for value functions: Vrπ​(s)=z⊤​ψπ​(s)V_{r}^{\pi}(s)=z^{\top}\psi^{\pi}(s), when defining ψπ(s)=𝔼a∼π(⋅|s)ψπ(s,a)\psi^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|s)}\psi^{\pi}(s,a). Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) generally11 1 There are BFMs that are not based on USFs. We refer the reader to Agarwal et al. (2025a) for a comprehensive overview. capitalize on the opportunity of evaluating policies for multiple reward functions, by additionally learning a family of parameterized policies (πz)z∈𝒵(\pi_{z})_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} with respect to all rewards in the span of features ϕ\phi (Borsa et al., 2018; Touati & Ollivier, 2021; Park et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025b). Concretely, BFMs train a family of parameterized policies so that each policy πz\pi_{z} is optimal for the reward function r⁡(s)=ϕ​(s)⊤​zr(s)=\phi(s)^{\top}z:

πz​(a|s)∈arg​maxa⁡ψπz​(s,a)⊤​zfor each ​z∈𝒵.\displaystyle\textstyle\pi_{z}(a|s)\in\argmax_{a}\psi^{\pi_{z}}(s,a)^{\top}z\quad\text{for each }z\in\mathcal{Z}. (3)

In practice, the set of policies, their SFs, and features ϕ\phi may be represented through function approximation: πz​(a|s)≈πξ​(a|s,z)\pi_{z}(a|s)\approx\pi_{\xi}(a|s,z), ψπz​(s,a)≈ψ⁡(s,a,z)\psi^{\pi_{z}}(s,a)\approx\psi(s,a,z), and ϕ⁡(s)≈ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s)\approx\phi(s). 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is a low-dimensional space, whose elements can be seen as task embeddings, as they represent reward functions in the feature basis. The low dimensionality of task embeddings is a key component enabling efficient task inference in this work.

Given a reward function rr at inference, the task embedding zrz_{r} parameterizing the optimal learned policy πzr\pi_{z_{r}} is found by minimizing the residual between r⁡(s)r(s) and ϕ​(s)⊤​z\phi(s)^{\top}z (i.e., projecting rr onto the span of ϕ\phi). Given a task inference dataset 𝒟=(si)i=1N\mathcal{D}=(s_{i})_{i=1}^{N} this may be solved in closed form:

zr=arg​minz⁡𝔼s∼𝒟​[(r⁡(s)−z⊤​ϕ​(s))2]=Cov𝒟​(ϕ)−1​𝔼s∼𝒟​[ϕ⁡(s)​r​(s)].\displaystyle\textstyle z_{r}=\argmin_{z}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}}[(r(s)-z^{\top}\phi(s))^{2}]=\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}}(\phi)^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}}[\phi(s)r(s)]. (4)

where Cov𝒟​(ϕ)−1=𝔼s,s′∼𝒟​[ϕ⁡(s)​ϕ​(s′)⊤]\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}}(\phi)^{-1}=\mathbb{E}_{s,s^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}}[\phi(s)\phi(s^{\prime})^{\top}]. This process of mapping from a reward function rr to an (approximately) optimal policy πzr\pi_{z_{r}} is what makes BFM based on USFs capable of zero-shot RL (Touati et al., 2023), i.e., they can produce an optimal policy for a previously unseen reward function. When the expectation over 𝒟\mathcal{D} is computed exactly, and rr lies in the span of ϕ\phi, then πzr\pi_{z_{r}} is guaranteed to be the optimal policy (Touati & Ollivier, 2021). However, in practice, the expectation is approximated through sampling, which requires (i) the availability of the task inference dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} (potentially a subset of the pre-training data) and (ii) providing reward labels for each state s∈𝒟s\in\mathcal{D}. As this can be an expensive operation, potentially requiring human supervision, we will propose an alternative online framework for retrieving zrz_{r}.

3 Optimistic Task Inference for Behavior Foundation Models

3.1 Setting: Task inference at Test-time

We consider an alternative framework for task inference in BFMs, designed to remove the necessity for storing pre-training data and, principally, to decrease the required number of reward labels. We focus on an online setting, in which the agent can update the task embedding zz during deployment, and directly control the collection of the data used to estimate zz. While the choice of zz will be uninformed at the beginning, it will ideally be possible to rapidly identify the correct task, and thus select the zz that retrieves the optimal policy, i.e., that coincides with the true task embedding.

More formally, we start from a pre-trained USF-based BFM, providing a set of parameterized policies (πz)z∈𝒵(\pi_{z})_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} , as well as SF estimates ψπz\psi^{\pi_{z}} of features ϕ\phi. While we will now consider finite-horizon SF estimates ψπz(s0)=∑t=0H−1γt𝔼[ϕ(st)|s0,πz]\psi^{\pi_{z}}(s_{0})=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\,\mathbb{E}\left[{\phi(s_{t})}\ \middle|\ {s_{0},\pi_{z}}\right] to streamline the presentation and analysis, we remark that the algorithm can be easily instantiated in infinite-horizon settings, as is done in our empirical evaluation. The agent interacts with the environment in an episodic setting with horizon HH and initial state distribution μ0\mu_{0}; instead of directly selecting actions, it will select a task embedding ztz_{t} at each step tt, and execute an action sampled from the respective policy at∼πzt(⋅|st)a_{t}\sim\pi_{z_{t}}(\cdot|s_{t}). This action will result in observing a new state st+1s_{t+1}, as well as the reward rtr_{t} of this transition, which constitutes the only source of information about the task22 2 We assume that each environment interaction provides a reward label; if the agent can additionally control when to request a reward label, more efficient schemes are possible, see Section B.2.

We define the discounted return of the kk-th episode as

G^k=∑t=0H−1γt​r​(sk​H+t).\displaystyle\hat{G}_{k}=\textstyle{\sum}_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}r(s_{kH+t}). (5)

where sk​H∼μ0s_{kH}\sim\mu_{0}, at∼πzt(⋅|st)a_{t}\sim\pi_{z_{t}}(\cdot|s_{t}) and st+1∼P(⋅|st,at)s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot|s_{t},a_{t}). The goal of the agent is now simply to minimize the expected regret over nn episodes

Rn=𝔼⁡[∑k=0n−1G^k⋆−G^k]\displaystyle R_{n}=\mathbb{E}\left[\textstyle{\sum}_{k=0}^{n-1}\ \hat{G}_{k}^{\star}-\hat{G}_{k}\right] (6)

where G^k⋆\hat{G}^{\star}_{k} denotes the discounted return choosing zrz_{r} in each step, and the expectation is w.r.t. μ0\mu_{0}, the MDP dynamics, the action distributions, and the choices of the task embeddings. Intuitively, the agent needs to follow a decision rule that maps the observed history of states and rewards to a task embedding: (s0,r0,…​st,rt)→zt+1∈𝒵(s_{0},r_{0},\dots s_{t},r_{t})\to z_{t+1}\in\mathcal{Z}. The selected task embeddings should induce informative trajectories with respect to the reward function, while largely avoiding suboptimal behavior. This setting is reminiscent of well-developed research directions, namely exploration in the space of behavioral priors (Singh et al., 2020) and fast adaptation (Sikchi et al., 2025); however, existing methods ignore the underlying structure connecting rewards and task embeddings, which we will show may be leveraged to efficiently achieve near-optimal performance.

3.2 Method: OpTI-BFM

Our method leverages a core feature of BFMs: for well-trained USFs, the expectation of the return of the kk-th episode (Eq. 5) from an initial state s0s_{0} is approximately linear w.r.t. the successor features of the policy conditioned on the kk-th task embedding zkz_{k}: ψ(s0,zk)⊤zr≈𝔼[G^k|s0,πzk]\psi(s_{0},z_{k})^{\top}z_{r}\approx\mathbb{E}[\hat{G}_{k}|s_{0},\pi_{z_{k}}], where zrz_{r} is the optimal task embedding, and initially unknown. This simple property has significant implication: Policy search reduces to online optimization of a linear function, which has been extensively studied in the bandit literature (Dani et al., 2008; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011). Building upon these fundamental results, we propose Optimistic Task Inference for BFMs (OpTI-BFM) in order to efficiently explore the space of behaviors while controlling suboptimality.

Interestingly, the same approximately linear relationship that connects SFs and returns, also exists between features and rewards: ϕ​(s)⊤​zr≈r⁡(s)\phi(s)^{\top}z_{r}\approx r(s). Following the latter property, OpTI-BFM keeps track of a least-squares estimate of zrz_{r} given the previously observed transitions

z^t=arg​minz∈𝒵∑i=0t(ri−ϕ(si)⊤z)2+λ‖z‖22=(λId+∑i=0tϕ(si)ϕ(si)⊤)−1∑i=0tϕ(si)ri\displaystyle\hat{z}_{t}=\argmin_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\sum_{i=0}^{t}\left(r_{i}-\phi(s_{i})^{\top}z\right)^{2}+\lambda\left\lVert{z}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}=\left(\lambda I_{d}+\sum_{i=0}^{t}\phi(s_{i})\phi(s_{i})^{\top}\right)^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{t}\phi(s_{i})\,r_{i} (7)

using l2l_{2}-regularization to ensure the inverse exists. Rewriting this as

z^t=Vt−1​∑i=0tϕ⁡(si)​ri,whereVt=λ​Id+∑i=0tϕ⁡(si)​ϕ​(si)⊤\displaystyle\hat{z}_{t}=V_{t}^{-1}\textstyle{\sum}_{i=0}^{t}\phi(s_{i})\,r_{i},\quad\text{where}\quad V_{t}=\lambda I_{d}+\textstyle{\sum}_{i=0}^{t}\phi(s_{i})\phi(s_{i})^{\top} (8)

allows OpTI-BFM to not only track the mean estimate z^t\hat{z}_{t}, but also a confidence ellipsoid 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} around z^t\hat{z}_{t} that contains the true task embedding zrz_{r} with high probability:

𝒞t={z∈ℝd:‖z−z^t−1‖Vt−1≤βt},\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{t}=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\big\|z-\hat{z}_{t-1}\big\|_{V_{t-1}}\leq\beta_{t}\right\}, (9)

where βt\beta_{t} controls the Mahalanobis distance. The estimation of confidence sets allows optimistic behavior in each step by choosing the task embedding ztz_{t} which is believed to attain the largest return among those in the confidence set:

zt∈arg​maxz∈𝒵⁡maxw∈𝒞t​w⊤​ψ​(st,z).\displaystyle z_{t}\in\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\max_{w\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\,w^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z). (10)

Intuitively, this procedure conditions the BFM on the most "promising" task embedding among those that are compatible with rewards observed so far. Note that this algorithm has one crucial difference to Upper Confidence Bound (UCB)-based algorithms for linear contextual bandits (Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011; Dani et al., 2008), as two different contexts are involved: the features ϕ\phi, which are used for online regression and for estimating the confidence interval, and the successor features ψ\psi, which are instead used in the acquisition function in Eq. 10. We will discuss that using ϕ\phi for regression results in tighter estimates in Section A.2.

Algorithm 1 instantiates OpTI-BFM for online task inference. We will establish guarantees for OpTI-BFM in the next section, and then describe how Eq. 10 may be optimized in practice, or avoided altogether with a Thompson Sampling (TS) variant, among others.

3.3 Guarantees

Leveraging a direct connection to principled algorithms for linear bandits (Dani et al., 2008; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011), we provide regret guarantees for OpTI-BFM. We note that this is a crucial property for online task inference, which could otherwise fail to gather informative data, and converge to suboptimal solutions. For simplicity, we study a variant of OpTI-BFM that only updates its decision rule at the beginning of each episode, i.e., we have zt=zt−1z_{t}=z_{t-1} for t∉{k​H}k=0∞t\notin\{kH\}_{k=0}^{\infty}33 3 We provide an empirical comparison to this variant in Section 5.3.. This additional constraint allows us to leverage results from linear contextual bandit literature.

We can show that OpTI-BFM approaches the performance of the optimal policy πzr\pi_{z_{r}} (Eq. 4) under the following assumptions:

  • (A1)

    Perfect USF for our setting: for every (s,a,z)∈𝒮×𝒜×𝒵(s,a,z)\in\mathcal{S\times A\times Z} we have ψ(s0,a0,z)=∑t=0H−1γt𝔼[ϕ(st)|πz,s0,a0] and πz(a|s)>0⟹a∈arg​maxa∈𝒜ψ(s,a,z)⊤z\psi(s_{0},a_{0},z)=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\mathbb{E}\left[{\phi(s_{t})}\ \middle|\ {\pi_{z},s_{0},a_{0}}\right]\text{ and }\pi_{z}(a|s)>0\implies a\in\argmax_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\psi(s,a,z)^{\top}z.

  • (A2)

    Linear Reward: rr is in the span of features ϕ\phi up to i.i.d. mean-zero σ\sigma-subgaussian noise ηt\eta_{t}, i.e. r⁡(st)=ϕ​(st)⊤​zr+ηtr(s_{t})=\phi(s_{t})^{\top}z_{r}+\eta_{t}

  • (A3)

    Optimization Oracle: the OpTI-BFM objective, Eq. 10, can be computed exactly.

  • (A4)

    Bounded norms: ‖zr‖2≤S\left\lVert{z_{r}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq S and ‖ϕ⁡(⋅)‖2≤L\left\lVert{\phi(\cdot)}\right\rVert_{2}\leq L for some S>0S>0 and L>0L>0.

Assumptions (A1) and (A2) are instrumental to recovering theoretical guarantees, but we found OpTI-BFM to perform well even when they are violated (see Section 5). Note that for a sufficiently large horizon HH the mismatch between the finite discounted sum of features we assume here and the infinite one we have in practice is negligible: the l2l_{2}-error is by L​γH/(1−γ)L\gamma^{H}/(1-\gamma). Assumption (A3) may be empirically motivated by the efficiency of finding a good approximate solution (see Section 4). In this setting, we can show that OpTI-BFM has sublinear regret.

Proposition 1.

(informal) Under assumptions A1-A4, in an episodic discounted MDP, if OpTI-BFM (Algorithm 1) only updates ztz_{t} at the start of each episode, it incurs an expected regret of Rn≤𝒪~​(d​n)R_{n}\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(d\sqrt{n}\right).

Proof.

We prove a formal version, Proposition 5, in Appendix A. The proof is similar to the standard regret bounds for LinUCB/OFUL (Dani et al., 2008; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011) except that the confidence interval is updated HH-times per step with features that differ from the context features of the bandit.∎

4 Practical Algorithm

Having introduced and analyzed OpTI-BFM, we now discuss a practical implementation, and present some additional variants 44 4 One additional variant is presented in Section B.2.

The main challenge for a practical implementation of OpTI-BFM lies in optimizing the decision criterion in Eq. 10, involving two continuous spaces 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}, and a highly non-linear map z↦ψ⁡(⋅,z)z\mapsto\psi(\cdot,z). Fortunately, BFMs are pre-trained such that that w≈arg​maxz∈𝒵⁡w⊤​ψ​(st,z)w\approx\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}w^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z), i.e. the optimal policy for a task described by ww is the one conditioned on ww itself. In practice, as training is not perfect, we do not strictly rely on this property, and still search zz over 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} instead of 𝒵\mathcal{Z}: 55 5 We additionally consider a radius of 2​βt2\beta_{t} instead of βt\beta_{t} for this confidence set.

zt∈arg​maxz∈𝒞t⁡maxw∈𝒞t​w⊤​ψ​(st,z)\displaystyle\textstyle z_{t}\in\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\max_{w\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\,w^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z) (11)

We note that, as 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} shrinks, so does the decision space, and with it the complexity of the optimization problem. Finally, as commonly done for linear UCB (Remark 1), we can reformulate the objective as

arg​maxz∈𝒞t⁡maxw∈𝒞t​w⊤​ψ​(st,z)=arg​maxz∈𝒞t⁡ψ​(st,z)⊤​z^t−1+βt​‖ψ⁡(st,z)‖Vt−1−1\displaystyle\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\max_{w\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\,w^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z)=\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\,\psi(s_{t},z)^{\top}\hat{z}_{t-1}+\beta_{t}\left\lVert{\psi(s_{t},z)}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}^{-1}} (12)

which allows us to optimize over just one variable. In practice, we found a simple sampling approach to be sufficient to find an approximate solution. We optimize the final objective through random shooting with a budget of n=128n=128 candidates, each of which is evaluated through a forward pass of the successor feature network ψ\psi in the BFM. Sampling from the ellipsoid 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t} may be done efficiently by applying the push-forward ξ↦z^t−1+Vt−1−1/2βtξ\xi\mapsto\hat{z}_{t-1}+V_{t-1}^{-1/2}\beta_{t}\xi to uniform samples from the unit ball (Barthe et al., 2005).

A practical implementation may also benefit from efficient updates to the key parameters: z^t−1\hat{z}_{t-1}, Vt−1−1/2V_{t-1}^{-1/2}, and Vt−1−1V_{t-1}^{-1}. We do so by keeping track of the information vector ∑s=1tϕt​rt\textstyle{\sum}_{s=1}^{t}\phi_{t}r_{t} and the Cholesky factor of VtV_{t}, i.e. Vt=Rt⊤​RtV_{t}=R_{t}^{\top}R_{t}. This enables updates and/or recomputation of all components in 𝒪⁡(d2)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}) (Gill et al., 1974; Seeger, 2004) making OpTI-BFM very cheap (see Section B.1).

Thompson Sampling Variant

The connection between least squares confidence sets and Bayesian linear regression is well established in contextual linear bandit literature (Kaufmann et al., 2012; Agrawal & Goyal, 2013). Concretely, we may interpret OpTI-BFM’s internal components at time-step tt as a Gaussian posterior 𝒩⁡(z^t−1,Vt−1−1)\mathcal{N}(\hat{z}_{t-1},V_{t-1}^{-1}) over task embeddings that stem from a Bayesian linear regression with prior 𝒩⁡(0,1λ​Id)\mathcal{N}(0,\tfrac{1}{\lambda}I_{d}) on the data {(ϕi/σ,ri/σ)}i=0t−1\{(\phi_{i}/\sigma,r_{i}/\sigma)\}_{i=0}^{t-1} (where σ\sigma is a hyper-parameter in practice). Intuitively, this can be thought of as starting from a prior on behaviors and then refining it over time until it converges to a single behavior. Given this Bayesian interpretation, it is then natural to consider a Thompson Sampling (TS) approach, where we simply sample a behavior from the posterior, i.e. task embedding zt∼𝒩⁡(z^t,Vt−1)z_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(\hat{z}_{t},V_{t}^{-1}), which foregoes the optimization of the UCB version. We evaluate this variant extensively in Section 5.

Non-stationary Rewards Variant

Because of its online nature, OpTI-BFM can potentially adapt to reward functions that change over time. To this end, we consider a variant leveraging a simple idea from non-stationary bandit literature: weighing old data points less than new ones in the least squares estimator (Russac et al., 2020). Concretely, we introduce a new hyper-parameter 0<ρ≤10<\rho\leq 1 and weight data from past time-step ss at time-step tt with weight ρt−s\rho^{t-s}. We evaluate OpTI-BFM in a setting with non-stationary rewards in Section 5.4.

5 Experiments

The empirical evaluation is divided in several subsections, each of which will address a specific question, as their titles suggest. In the following, we first detail some evaluation choices.

Environments

To evaluate performance of various adaptation/inference algorithms we consider the environments Walker, Cheetah, and Quadruped from the established ExORL (Yarats et al., 2022) benchmark, with four different tasks (i.e. reward functions) each. We describe full experimental protocols in Appendix E. In all figures, error-bars and shaded regions represent min-max-intervals over 3 training seeds.

Methods

We choose Forward-Backward (FB) framework (Touati & Ollivier, 2021) as a state-of-the-art BFM. We adhere to the standard training and evaluation protocol for FB (Touati et al., 2023), and described it in detail in Appendix D. We apply OpTI-BFM on top of this BFM, as well as a Thompson-Sampling variant, OpTI-BFM-TS. We further consider LoLA (Sikchi et al., 2025), an approach based on policy search that was originally introduced for fast adaptation. In compliance with our online task inference setting, we initialize LoLA with an uninformed choice of zz, and estimate on-policy returns in the standard episodic fashion, without privileged resets. Besides these three learning algorithms, we evaluate “Random” and “Oracle” baselines that serve as a lower and an upper bound on possible performance respectively. The former executes a random embedding in each step, i.e. zt∼Unif​(𝒵)z_{t}\sim\text{Unif}(\mathcal{Z}), whereas the latter executes the optimal policy πzr\pi_{z_{r}}, where zrz_{r} is attained by solving the linear regression problem in Eq. 4, assuming privileged access to labeled data or the reward function. We follow standard practice and approximate zrz_{r} with a large budget of 50k labeled samples from the pre-training dataset in practice (Touati et al., 2023; Agarwal et al., 2025b). If not indicated otherwise, “relative performance” is relative to the Oracle performance.

5.1 How does OpTI-BFM compare to other online task inference methods?

We first evaluate all methods in the online task inference setting described in Section 3.1, and report episodic returns (Eq. 5) in Fig. 2. We find that OpTI-BFM recovers Oracle performance on all tasks within 5 episodes (5k environment steps) of interaction. We observe a significant gap between the optimistic strategy of OpTI-BFM and its TS variant in Cheetah. Nevertheless, TS remains a promising approach, as it avoids any optimization problem, and simply samples task embeddings from its current belief. Finally, we find that LoLA, which ignores the linear structure of the problem and performs blackbox policy search, makes slower progress which is better visible over 50 episodes in Fig. 10 in Appendix C. This result is consistent with existing ablations initializing LoLA to a random task embedding (see Sikchi et al. (2025), Figure 5), as is the case in our setting.

5.2 Is the data collected actively by OpTI-BFM informative?

While the previous evaluations focus on episodic returns, or equivalently regret minimization, we now evaluate the quality of the inferred task embeddings, e.g., in the case of OpTI-BFM, how well does πz^n\pi_{\hat{z}_{n}} perform? In practice, to ablate away any bias in l2l_{2}-regularized estimators, we compute the task embedding znz_{n} by minimizing the squared error in Eq. 4 over the dataset of the first nn observed transitions of each method, and evaluate the corresponding policy πzn\pi_{z_{n}} in the same environment and task. We compare with two baseline data sources: (i) random trajectories from RND (Burda et al., 2018), which represents a task-agnostic exploration approach, and (ii) the first nn samples from our Random baseline, which rolls out a random policy learned by the BFM. Figure 3 shows the average relative performance of πzn\pi_{z_{n}} in each environment. We find that the data from an actively exploring source, i.e. OpTI-BFM and RND, outperforms the passive Random approach. Furthermore, we can see that OpTI-BFM and its TS variant tend to be more data-efficient than RND, which can be traced back to task-awareness.

5.3 Are frequent updates important?

The regret bound provided in Section 3.3 assumes a version of OpTI-BFM that only updates the task embedding it executes at the start of each episode. In this section we aim to experimentally quantify this gap in theory and practice by evaluating this episodic version of OpTI-BFM. Fig. 4 shows that changing the latent on an episode-level leads to slower improvement than changing every step. The episodic versions do reach equal performance eventually as shown in Fig. 10 in Appendix C.

5.4 Can OpTI-BFM adapt to non-stationary rewards?

It is conceivable that OpTI-BFM can adapt to reward functions that are changing over time because of its online nature. To investigate whether this is possible, we introduce two new tasks for the Walker environment that closely resemble the walk and run tasks but change the velocity target over time: speedup and slowdown increase and decrease the velocity target respectively after an initial “burn-in” phase. We evaluate OpTI-BFM in a single, 30k-step, episode in Figure 5, which shows that a direct application of OpTI-BFM (ρ=1.0\rho=1.0) struggles to adapt to the changing reward function after converging to a fixed one in the first 10k steps. As soon as ρ\rho is reduced, OpTI-BFM tracks the velocity target more accurately. Moreover, we observe that, if ρ\rho is too small, the uncertainty is not reduced quickly enough, and the agent can converge to suboptimal behavior.

5.5 Can OpTI-BFM warm-start from labeled data?

In settings that provide a small amount of labeled data 𝒟={(si,ri)}i=1n\mathcal{D}=\{(s_{i},r_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} from the beginning (Sikchi et al., 2025), OpTI-BFM may be warm-started by updating the least squares estimator nn-times with the given data. As shown in Fig. 6, when doing so on high-quality i.i.d. data from the training dataset, the performance of OpTI-BFM quickly improves, showing that OpTI-BFM can additionally be seen an extension of the traditional task inference of BFMs.

6 Related Work

Behavior Foundation Models

This work builds upon USFs (Dayan, 1993; Barreto et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2020), and specifically on BFMs that utilize SFs to train a parameterized policy and the corresponding parameterized SFs. A common approach for learning SF-based BFMs is to approximate of successor measures (Blier et al., 2021; Touati & Ollivier, 2021; Agarwal et al., 2025b), but other options spanning from spectral decomposition of random visitations (Wu et al., 2018) to implicit value learning (Park et al., 2024) also exist. In this regard, we refer the reader to Agarwal et al. (2025a) for a broader overview of BFMs and unsupervised RL. Among these approaches, the Forward Backward (FB) framework (Touati & Ollivier, 2021) has risen to prominence, as it achieves state-of-the-art performance in standard continuous control tasks (Touati et al., 2023), while being scalable to humanoid control (Tirinzoni et al., 2025). Recent work has explored various applications of FB’s zero-shot capabilities, such as imitation learning (Pirotta et al., 2023), epistemic exploration (Urpí et al., 2025), and constrained RL (Hugessen et al., 2025). Among related works, our method is most closely related to Sikchi et al. (2025), which however focuses on a different problem: fine-tuning a zero-shot policy, which is already initialized through standard offline task inference. On the other hand, our goal is to find a strong policy purely through environment interaction, without relying on preexisting labeled data. The two approaches might nevertheless be combined.

Reward Learning

The task inference goal of OpTI-BFM is fundamentally connected to the reward learning problem in RL. Among the many instantiations, rewards may be inferred from scalar evaluations (Knox & Stone, 2009; MacGlashan et al., 2017), preferences (Fürnkranz et al., 2012; Christiano et al., 2017), or from other types of feedback (Jeon et al., 2020). A powerful extension to reward learning explores active strategies for query selection, largely adopting a Bayesian perspective (Bıyık et al., 2020; Wilde et al., 2020). While none of these works are aimed at BFMs, several are close in spirit: for instance, Lindner et al. (2021) propose an information-directed method to achieve a similar goal to ours: inferring the task in a way which does not necessarily reduce the model error, but quickly produces an optimal policy.

Linear Bandits

Linear Contextual Bandits are a well-studied problem in bandit literature (Abe & Long, 1999; Dani et al., 2008; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011; Kaufmann et al., 2012; Agrawal & Goyal, 2013). This is influential to this work in two ways. First, OpTI-BFM is inspired by UCB methods in this setting (Dani et al., 2008; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011). Second, we utilize guarantees and ideas from this literature (Lattimore & Szepesvári, 2020) to produce a regret bound for OpTI-BFM in an episodic setting.

7 Conclusion

By drawing a connection between practical work in scalable Behavior Foundation Models and rigorous algorithms for linear optimization, we proposed an algorithm that may efficiently infer the task at hand and retrieve a well-performing policy in high-dimensional, complex environments. By minimizing the number of reward evaluations necessary for task inference, this algorithm can enable BFM to be applied beyond domains in which rewards are readily available, for instance when learning directly from pixels.

OpTI-BFM is designed to perform task inference in a minimal number of episodes: this is mainly possible as the search space is minimal. While updating the task embedding alone enables great sample efficiency, fine-tuning additional components of the BFM may provide even better performance in the long run (Sikchi et al., 2025).

While OpTI-BFM builds upon linearity between features and rewards, it does not make any significant assumption on the structure of the feature space 𝒵\mathcal{Z}: understanding the properties of its elements both formally and practically constitutes an important avenue for future work. BFMs have demonstrated scalability up to complex domains, while maintaining structured properties (linearity!) in an embedding space: we believe that this is a ripe field for application of more theoretically principled approaches, which may in turn be impactful beyond regular domains.

Appendix A Proofs

This section describes the proof for Proposition 1. It closely follows Chapters 19 and 20 from Lattimore & Szepesvári (2020). We proceed as follows:

  • •

    We reintroduce the setting with some more convenient notation in Section A.1.

  • •

    We show that running linear regression on feature-reward pairs is at least as efficient as running linear regression on SF-return pairs (Section A.2)

  • •

    We cite a result that grants the optimal choice of β\betas in Section A.3.

  • •

    We proceed with the standard linear contextual bandit regret bound proof with confidence sets based on feature-reward pairs (Section A.4).

A.1 Setting

Throughout this section we will use the double subscript k,tk,t to denote the tt-th time-step in the kk episode. Since we will analyze a version of OpTI-BFM that only switches task embedding at the start of each episode, and since we know that the best task embedding is always zrz_{r} (Eq. 4), we define z1,…,znz_{1},\dots,z_{n} be the chosen task embeddings for nn episodes. Let ϕk,t=ϕ⁡(sk,t)\phi_{k,t}=\phi(s_{k,t}) be the feature observed in step tt of episode kk. Note that this quantity is a random variable; throughout this section we use a simple expectation 𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}[\cdot] to indicate the expectation over initial states, action distributions of policies, MDP dynamics, and decisions of the algorithm. We will still use 𝔼[⋅|π,s]\mathbb{E}\left[{\cdot}\ \middle|\ {\pi,s}\right] to denote the expectation over rolling out policy π\pi from state ss.

For convenience, we repeat our assumptions here with the new notation

=𝔼[∑t=0H−1γtrk,t|πz,sk,0]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[{\textstyle{\sum}_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}r_{k,t}}\ \middle|\ {\pi_{z},s_{k,0}}\right] (20)
=𝔼[∑t=0H−1γt⟨zr,ϕ(sk,t)⟩|πz,sk,0]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[{\textstyle{\sum}_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\langle z_{r},\phi(s_{k,t})\rangle}\ \middle|\ {\pi_{z},s_{k,0}}\right] (21)
=⟨zr,𝔼[∑t=0H−1γtϕ(sk,t)|πz,sk,0]⟩\displaystyle=\left\langle z_{r},\mathbb{E}\left[{\textstyle{\sum}_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\phi(s_{k,t})}\ \middle|\ {\pi_{z},s_{k,0}}\right]\right\rangle (22)
=A​1⟨zr,ψ⁡(sk,0,z)⟩\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle A1}}{{=}}\langle z_{r},\psi(s_{k,0},z)\rangle (23)

Thus, our setting resembles a contextual bandit with context s0∼μ0s_{0}\sim\mu_{0}, action space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} and an expected payoff that is linear in ψ⁡(s0,z)\psi(s_{0},z), with the one notable difference being that more information is available on the pay-off feedback: it is not available in terms of return G^k\hat{G}_{k} alone, but additionally as a sequence of features-reward pairs (ϕk,t,rk,t)t=0H−1(\phi_{k,t},r_{k,t})_{t=0}^{H-1}.

A.1.3 OpTI-BFM

Let us finally reintroduce the least squares estimator with the double subscript notation:

z^n=Vn−1​∑k=1n∑t=0H−1ϕk,t​rk,twhereVn=λ​I+∑k=1n∑t=0H−1ϕk,t​ϕk,t⊤.\displaystyle\hat{z}_{n}=V_{n}^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\phi_{k,t}r_{k,t}\quad\text{where}\quad V_{n}=\lambda I+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\phi_{k,t}\phi_{k,t}^{\top}. (24)

From this we then redefine the confidence sets at the start of episode kk as

𝒞k={z∈ℝd:‖z−z^k−1‖Vk−1≤βk}.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{k}=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\left\lVert{z-\hat{z}_{k-1}}\right\rVert_{V_{k-1}}\leq\beta_{k}\}. (25)

Defining the UCB operator as

UCBk​(z)=maxw∈𝒞k⁡⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,z),w⟩,\displaystyle\text{UCB}_{k}(z)=\max_{w\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z),w\rangle, (26)

then OpTI-BFM picks zk=arg​max𝒵⁡UCBk​(z)z_{k}=\argmax_{\mathcal{Z}}\text{UCB}_{k}(z) for the kk-th episode, which we assume can be attained exactly in A3.

A.2 Return-level vs. Reward-level feedback

In this section we show a few properties conveying the intuitive fact that, if zrz_{r} is estimated from richer, reward-level feedback (ϕk,t,rk,t)(\phi_{k,t},r_{k,t}), confidence sets may be tigher than those produced by return-level feedback (∑t=0H−1γt​ϕk,t,∑t=0H−1γt​rk,t)(\textstyle{\sum}_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\phi_{k,t},\textstyle{\sum}_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}r_{k,t}), which can be though of as an aggregation of HH datapoints of the former (up to expectation over dynamics).

For this analysis we define the empirical SF of episode kk as

ψ~k=∑t=0H−1γt​ϕk,tandWn\displaystyle\tilde{\psi}_{k}=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\phi_{k,t}\quad\text{and}\quad W_{n} =λ​I+∑k=1nψ~k​ψ~k⊤.\displaystyle=\lambda I+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\tilde{\psi}_{k}\tilde{\psi}_{k}^{\top}. (27)

Note that we have 𝔼[ψ~k|πzk,sk,0]=ψ(sk,0,zk)\mathbb{E}\left[{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\pi_{z_{k}},s_{k,0}}\right]=\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k}). We further define

Ak=∑t=0H−1ϕk,t​ϕk,t⊤,\displaystyle A_{k}=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\phi_{k,t}\phi_{k,t}^{\top}, (28)

so that we have Vn=λ​I+∑k=1nAkV_{n}=\lambda I+\sum_{k=1}^{n}A_{k}. Finally, the following constant 66 6 Note that cH≥1c_{H}\geq 1 for H>0H>0. will become useful later:

cH=∑t=0H−1γ2​t=1−γ2​H1−γ2.\displaystyle c_{H}=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{2t}=\frac{1-\gamma^{2H}}{1-\gamma^{2}}. (29)

We now show that the precision matrices obtained through reward-level feedback (VnV_{n}) grow at least as fast as those obtained through return-level feedback (WnW_{n}) over the course of one episode.

Proposition 2.

We have, in Loewner order,

ψ~k​ψ~k⊤≼cH​Ak.\displaystyle\tilde{\psi}_{k}\tilde{\psi}_{k}^{\top}\preccurlyeq c_{H}A_{k}. (30)
Proof.

This is a direct application of a Cauchy-Schwarz inequality: for any xx,

x⊤​ψ~k​ψ~k⊤​x=(x⊤​ψ~k)2=(∑t=0H−1γt​x⊤​ϕk,t)2≤(∑t=0H−1γ2​t)​(∑t=0H−1(x⊤​ϕk,t)2)=cH​x⊤​Ak​x\displaystyle x^{\top}\tilde{\psi}_{k}\tilde{\psi}_{k}^{\top}x=(x^{\top}\tilde{\psi}_{k})^{2}=\left(\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}x^{\top}\phi_{k,t}\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{2t}\right)\left(\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}(x^{\top}\phi_{k,t})^{2}\right)=c_{H}x^{\top}A_{k}x

∎

From this, it immediately follows VnV_{n} grows at least as fast as WnW_{n} over all episodes.

Proposition 3.

We have, in Loewner order,

Vn≽1cH​Wn\displaystyle V_{n}\succcurlyeq\frac{1}{c_{H}}W_{n} (31)
Proof.

Using Proposition 2, we know that

Ak≽1cH​ψ~k​ψ~k⊤.\displaystyle A_{k}\succcurlyeq\frac{1}{c_{H}}\tilde{\psi}_{k}\tilde{\psi}_{k}^{\top}. (32)

Summing over episodes on both sides, we get

∑k=1nAk≽1cH​∑k=1nψ~k​ψ~k⊤.\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}A_{k}\succcurlyeq\frac{1}{c_{H}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\tilde{\psi}_{k}\tilde{\psi}_{k}^{\top}. (33)

By adding λ​I\lambda I on both sides, we can write

λ​I+∑k=1nAk≽λ​I+1cH​∑k=1nψ~k​ψ~k⊤.\displaystyle\lambda I+\sum_{k=1}^{n}A_{k}\succcurlyeq\lambda I+\frac{1}{c_{H}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\tilde{\psi}_{k}\tilde{\psi}_{k}^{\top}. (34)

On the left, we recognize

λ​I+∑k=1nAk=Vn,\displaystyle\lambda I+\sum_{k=1}^{n}A_{k}=V_{n}, (35)

while on the right we have

λ​I+1cH​∑k=1nψ~k​ψ~k⊤=1cH​(λ​I+∑k=1nψ~k​ψ~k⊤)+(1−1cH)​λ​I=1cH​Wn+(1−1cH)​λ​I,\displaystyle\lambda I+\frac{1}{c_{H}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\tilde{\psi}_{k}\tilde{\psi}_{k}^{\top}=\frac{1}{c_{H}}\left(\lambda I+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\tilde{\psi}_{k}\tilde{\psi}_{k}^{\top}\right)+\left(1-\frac{1}{c_{H}}\right)\lambda I=\frac{1}{c_{H}}W_{n}+\left(1-\frac{1}{c_{H}}\right)\lambda I,

which in turn yields

Vn≽1cH​Wn+(1−1cH)​λ​I≽1cH​Wn,\displaystyle V_{n}\succcurlyeq\frac{1}{c_{H}}W_{n}+\left(1-\frac{1}{c_{H}}\right)\lambda I\succcurlyeq\frac{1}{c_{H}}W_{n}, (36)

where the last step follows from the fact that cH≥1c_{H}\geq 1. ∎

We now derive a useful property from this result, that will later help us to apply the well-known elliptical potential Lemma. Intuitively it shows that reward-level feedback leads to confidence ellipsoids at least as tight as those of return-level feedback.

Proposition 4.

We have for any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}

‖x‖Vn−1≤cH​‖x‖Wn−1\displaystyle\left\lVert{x}\right\rVert_{V_{n}^{-1}}\leq\sqrt{c_{H}}\left\lVert{x}\right\rVert_{W_{n}^{-1}} (37)
Proof.

By Proposition 3,

Vn≽1cH​Wn,\displaystyle V_{n}\succcurlyeq\frac{1}{c_{H}}W_{n}, (38)

where both matrices are positive definite by construction. As the inverse thus reverses order,

Vn−1≼cH​Wn−1.\displaystyle V_{n}^{-1}\preccurlyeq c_{H}W_{n}^{-1}. (39)

As a consequence, one can show that, for any xx,

‖x‖Vn−1=x⊤​Vn−1​x≤cH​x⊤​Wn−1​x=cH​‖x‖Wn−1.\displaystyle\left\lVert{x}\right\rVert_{V_{n}^{-1}}=\sqrt{x^{\top}V_{n}^{-1}x}\leq\sqrt{c_{H}x^{\top}W_{n}^{-1}x}=\sqrt{c_{H}}\left\lVert{x}\right\rVert_{W_{n}^{-1}}. (40)

∎

A.3 Confidence Ellipsoids

We will now take take the chance to cite a standard result for optimal choices of radii βk\beta_{k} which guarantee that the true parameter zrz_{r} is contained in confidence sets (Eq. 9)in each time-step with high probability.

Theorem 1.

(Adapted from Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) Theorem 2)
Given confidence sets 𝒞k\mathcal{C}_{k} as defined in Eq. 25, and if rewards are in the span of ϕ\phi up to σ\sigma-subgaussian zero-mean noise (A2), then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) the following holds: Pr⁡[∃k∈ℕ+|zr∉𝒞k]≤δ\Pr[\exists k\in\mathbb{N}^{+}|z_{r}\notin\mathcal{C}_{k}]\leq\delta with

βk=λ​S+σ​log⁡(detVk−1λd)+2​log⁡(1δ)\displaystyle\beta_{k}=\sqrt{\lambda}S+\sigma\sqrt{\log\left(\frac{\det V_{k-1}}{\lambda^{d}}\right)+2\log\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)} (41)

This is the classic uniform-in-time self-normalized bound based on supermartingales. Notice that the theorem makes no assumptions about the action selection process nor the process that controls the state-changes, except that they are measurable in the natural filtration of the corresponding time-step, which is the case for our decision rule (OpTI-BFM) and our episodic MDP setting. We remark that, since by definition Vt≽VsV_{t}\succcurlyeq V_{s} for all t≥st\geq s, we have that βt≥βs\beta_{t}\geq\beta_{s} as well.

A.4 Regret Bound

We can now prove a formal version of Proposition 1.

Proposition 5.

Under assumptions A1-A4, with choices for βk\beta_{k} as in Theorem 1, if OpTI-BFM is applied at the beginning of each episode and selects the task embedding zk=arg​max𝒵⁡UCBk​(z)z_{k}=\argmax_{\mathcal{Z}}\text{UCB}_{k}(z) for the kk-th episode, it incurs an expected regret of 𝒪~​(d​n)\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{n}).

Proof.

We start off by investigating the event ℰ\mathcal{E} that zr∈𝒞k​∀k∈{1,…,n}z_{r}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}\,\forall k\in\{1,\dots,n\}, i.e., zrz_{r} is in all confidence sets, which occurs with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta according to Theorem 1.

Since we will refer to both empirical and "expected" SFs (ψ~\tilde{\psi} and ψ\psi, respectively), we introduce the natural filtration ℱk−1\mathcal{F}_{k-1} generated by the history up to the start of episode kk, in particular, sk,0,zk,Vk−1,Wk−1s_{k,0},z_{k},V_{k-1},W_{k-1} are ℱk−1\mathcal{F}_{k-1}-measurable. Intuitively, conditioning on ℱk−1\mathcal{F}_{k-1} allows us to limit randomness to within the current episode. Crucial for us will be,

ψ⁡(sk,0,zk)=𝔼⁡[ψ~k|ℱk−1]\displaystyle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k})=\mathbb{E}\left[{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right] (42)

We will proceed as in the standard regret bound for linear contextual bandits (Lattimore & Szepesvári, 2020) Let z~k=arg​maxw∈𝒞k⁡⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zk),w⟩\tilde{z}_{k}=\argmax_{w\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k}),w\rangle be the task embedding that maximizes the UCB. We then have that

⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zr),zr⟩≤UCBk​(zr)≤UCBk​(zk)=⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zk),z~k⟩.\displaystyle\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{r}),z_{r}\rangle\leq\text{UCB}_{k}(z_{r})\leq\text{UCB}_{k}(z_{k})=\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k}),\tilde{z}_{k}\rangle. (43)

We can therefore bound the instantaneous regret eke_{k} by

ek\displaystyle e_{k} =Gk,zr−Gk,zk\displaystyle=G_{k,z_{r}}-G_{k,z_{k}} (44)
=⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zr),zr⟩−⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zk),zr⟩\displaystyle=\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{r}),z_{r}\rangle-\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k}),z_{r}\rangle (45)
≤⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zk),z~k⟩−⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zk),zr⟩\displaystyle\leq\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k}),\tilde{z}_{k}\rangle-\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k}),z_{r}\rangle (46)
=⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zk),z~k−zr⟩.\displaystyle=\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k}),\tilde{z}_{k}-z_{r}\rangle. (47)

Conditioning on previous events (ℱk−1\mathcal{F}_{k-1}), and applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality pointwise, we have

𝔼⁡[ek|ℱk−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right] ≤𝔼⁡[⟨ψ⁡(sk,0,zk),z~k−zr⟩|ℱk−1]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[{\langle\psi(s_{k,0},z_{k}),\tilde{z}_{k}-z_{r}\rangle}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right] (48)
=𝔼⁡[⟨ψ~k,z~k−zr⟩|ℱk−1]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[{\langle\tilde{\psi}_{k},\tilde{z}_{k}-z_{r}\rangle}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right] (49)
≤𝔼⁡[‖ψ~k‖Vk−1−1​‖z~k−zr‖Vk−1|ℱk−1].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[{\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{V_{k-1}^{-1}}\left\lVert{\tilde{z}_{k}-z_{r}}\right\rVert_{V_{k-1}}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]. (50)

Since we are in event ℰ\mathcal{E} we have zr∈𝒞kz_{r}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}, furthermore, z~k∈𝒞k\tilde{z}_{k}\in\mathcal{C}_{k} by definition. So, using the definition of the confidence set Eq. 25, we have

‖z~k−zr‖Vk−1≤2​βk≤2​βn.\displaystyle\left\lVert{\tilde{z}_{k}-z_{r}}\right\rVert_{V_{k-1}}\leq 2\beta_{k}\leq 2\beta_{n}. (51)

This is where this proof diverges from the standard regret bound: note that Vk−1V_{k-1} is a sum of features ϕ\phi and not empirical SFs ψ~\tilde{\psi}, making immediate application of the elliptical potential lemma non-trivial. We can however recall the comparison of least square estimation with reward-feedback and return-feedback from Section A.2. In particular, one can apply Proposition 4 to upper-bound the VV-norm with the WW-norm that depends on the empirical SFs:

‖ψ~k‖Vk−1−1≤cH​‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1.\displaystyle\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{V_{k-1}^{-1}}\leq\sqrt{c_{H}}\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}. (52)

Combining these two bounds results in

𝔼⁡[ek|ℱk−1]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right] ≤𝔼⁡[2​βn​cH​‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1|ℱk−1].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[{2\beta_{n}\sqrt{c_{H}}\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]. (53)

Recalling that, by assumption A4, ‖ψ~k‖2≤L⁡(1−γH)1−γ\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{L(1-\gamma^{H})}{1-\gamma} and

Vk−1=λ​I+∑i=1k∑t=0H−1ϕi,t​ϕi,t⊤≽λ​I\displaystyle V_{k-1}=\lambda I+\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\phi_{i,t}\phi_{i,t}^{\top}\,\succcurlyeq\,\lambda I (54)

so ‖u‖≤λ−1/2‖u‖Vk−1\left\lVert{u}\right\rVert\leq\lambda^{-1/2}\left\lVert{u}\right\rVert_{V_{k-1}}, we can write that, pointwise for all kk,

|⟨ψ~k,z~k−zr⟩|\displaystyle\left|\left\langle\tilde{\psi}_{k},\,\tilde{z}_{k}-z_{r}\right\rangle\right| ≤min⁡{2​βnλ​‖ψ~k‖, 2​βn​cH​‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1}\displaystyle\leq\min\left\{\frac{2\beta_{n}}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert,\;2\beta_{n}\sqrt{c_{H}}\,\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}\right\} (55)
≤2βnmin{L⁡(1−γH)λ​(1−γ)⏟=:B,cH‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1}.\displaystyle\leq 2\beta_{n}\min\left\{\underbrace{\frac{L(1-\gamma^{H})}{\sqrt{\lambda}(1-\gamma)}}_{=:B},\;\sqrt{c_{H}}\,\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}\right\}. (56)

Combining the two bounds inside the expectation (as they hold pointwise), we obtain

𝔼⁡[ek|ℱk−1]≤𝔼⁡[2​βn​min⁡{B,cH​‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1}|ℱk−1].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[{2\beta_{n}\min\left\{B,\sqrt{c_{H}}\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}\right\}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]. (57)

Using the fact that min⁡{a,b​x}≤max⁡{a,b}​min​{1,x}\min\{a,bx\}\leq\max\{a,b\}\min\{1,x\} for a,b>0a,b>0, we can then take some constants out of the expectation:

𝔼[ek|ℱk−1]≤max⁡{B,cH}⏟=:α𝔼[2βnmin{1,‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1}|ℱk−1].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]\leq\underbrace{\max\{B,\sqrt{c_{H}}\}}_{=:\alpha}\,\mathbb{E}\left[{2\beta_{n}\min\left\{1,\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}\right\}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]. (58)

We now sum over episodes. To do this, we use the tower rule on eke_{k}, i.e., 𝔼⁡[ek]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[ek|ℱk−1]]\mathbb{E}[e_{k}]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]].

Rn=𝔼⁡[∑k=1nek]=∑k=1n𝔼⁡[ek]=∑k=1n𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[ek|ℱk−1]]\displaystyle R_{n}=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{n}e_{k}\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[e_{k}\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]\big] (59)

Applying our (pointwise) bound on 𝔼⁡[ek|ℱk−1]\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right] and the tower rule again, we get.

Rn=∑k=1n𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[ek|ℱk−1]]\displaystyle R_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbb{E}\left[{e_{k}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]\big] ≤2​α​∑k=1n𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[βn​min⁡{1,‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1}|ℱk−1]]\displaystyle\leq 2\alpha\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}\left[{\beta_{n}\min\left\{1,\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}\right\}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{F}_{k-1}}\right]\right] (60)
=2​α​∑k=1n𝔼⁡[βn​min⁡{1,‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1}].\displaystyle=2\alpha\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[\beta_{n}\min\left\{1,\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}\right\}\right]. (61)

Using linearity of expectation and then applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality over episodes (pointwise), we can prepare the sum to the application of the elliptical potential Lemma on (ψ~k)k=1n(\tilde{\psi}_{k})_{k=1}^{n} and (Wk)k=1n(W_{k})_{k=1}^{n} (pathwise):

Rn\displaystyle R_{n} ≤2​α​𝔼​[βn​∑k=1nmin⁡{1,‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−1}]\displaystyle\leq 2\alpha\,\mathbb{E}\left[\beta_{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\min\left\{1,\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}\right\}\right] (62)
≤2​α​𝔼​[βn​n⋅∑k=1nmin⁡{1,‖ψ~k‖Wk−1−12}]\displaystyle\leq 2\alpha\,\mathbb{E}\left[\beta_{n}\sqrt{n\cdot\sum_{k=1}^{n}\min\left\{1,\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert^{2}_{W_{k-1}^{-1}}\right\}}\right] (63)
≤2​α​𝔼​[βn​2​n⋅log⁡(detWnλd)].\displaystyle\leq 2\alpha\,\mathbb{E}\left[\beta_{n}\sqrt{2n\cdot\log\left(\frac{\det W_{n}}{\lambda^{d}}\right)}\right]. (64)

Inserting our choice for βn\beta_{n} we obtain

Rn≤2​α​𝔼​[(λ​S+σ⁡(log⁡(detVn−1λd)+2​log⁡(1/δ)))​2​n⋅log⁡(detWnλd)]\displaystyle R_{n}\leq 2\alpha\,\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sqrt{\lambda}S+\sigma\left(\sqrt{\log\left(\frac{\det V_{n-1}}{\lambda^{d}}\right)+2\log(1/\delta)}\right)\right)\sqrt{2n\cdot\log\left(\frac{\det W_{n}}{\lambda^{d}}\right)}\right] (65)

We recall that, so far, we investigated the expected regret conditional on the event ℰ\mathcal{E} that zr∈𝒞k​∀k∈{1,…,n}z_{r}\in\mathcal{C}_{k}\,\forall k\in\{1,\dots,n\}, which occurs with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta according to Theorem 1. We now choose δ=1/n\delta=1/n. Using Proposition 6 to upper-bound the determinants (pointwise), and recalling the fact that ‖ψ~k‖2≤L⁡(1−γH)1−γ\left\lVert{\tilde{\psi}_{k}}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\frac{L(1-\gamma^{H})}{1-\gamma} (by A4), we obtain

Rn\displaystyle R_{n} ≤2​α​(λ​S+σ⁡(d​log⁡(d​λ+n​H​L2d​λ)+2​log⁡n))​2​n​d​log⁡(d​λ+n​L2​(1−γH)2(1−γ)2d​λ)\displaystyle\leq 2\alpha\left(\sqrt{\lambda}S+\sigma\left(\sqrt{d\log\left(\frac{d\lambda+nHL^{2}}{d\lambda}\right)+2\log n}\right)\right)\sqrt{2nd\log\left(\frac{d\lambda+n\frac{L^{2}(1-\gamma^{H})^{2}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}}{d\lambda}\right)}
≤𝒪~​(d​n).\displaystyle\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(d\sqrt{n}\right). (66)

We finally investigate the complementary event ℰC\mathcal{E}^{C}. We remark that the discounted return in each episode can be bounded by constants using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality:

|Gk,z|=|𝔼[∑t=0H−1γtϕk,t⊤zr|πzk,sk,0]|≤LS∑t=0H−1γt≤L​S1−γ.\displaystyle|G_{k,z}|=\left|\mathbb{E}\left[{\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\phi_{k,t}^{\top}z_{r}}\ \middle|\ {\pi_{z_{k}},s_{k,0}}\right]\right|\leq LS\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\gamma^{t}\leq\frac{LS}{1-\gamma}. (67)

It thus holds that Rn≤n⋅2​L​S1−γR_{n}\leq n\cdot\frac{2LS}{1-\gamma} under ℰC\mathcal{E}^{C}.

To combine the analysis for both events, let R^n=∑k=1nek\hat{R}_{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}e_{k} be the empirical regret. By the law of total probability, we have that

Rn=𝔼⁡[R^n]\displaystyle R_{n}=\mathbb{E}[\hat{R}_{n}] =Pr⁡[ℰ]⋅𝔼⁡[R^n|ℰ]+Pr⁡[ℰC]⋅𝔼⁡[R^n|ℰC]\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathcal{E}]\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[{\hat{R}_{n}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{E}}\right]+\Pr[\mathcal{E}^{C}]\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[{\hat{R}_{n}}\ \middle|\ {\mathcal{E}^{C}}\right] (68)
≤1⋅𝒪~​(d​n)+1n⋅n⋅2​L​S1−γ\displaystyle\leq 1\cdot\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(d\sqrt{n}\right)+\frac{1}{n}\cdot n\cdot\frac{2LS}{1-\gamma} (69)
≤𝒪~​(d​n),\displaystyle\leq\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(d\sqrt{n}\right), (70)

which concludes the proof. ∎

Let ϕ1,…,ϕn\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n} be a sequence of vectors with ‖ϕt‖≤L\left\lVert{\phi_{t}}\right\rVert\leq L for all t=1,…,nt=1,\dots,n, and Vt=λ​I+∑s=1tϕs​ϕs⊤V_{t}=\lambda I+\sum_{s=1}^{t}\phi_{s}\phi_{s}^{\top}.

log⁡(detVnλd)≤d​log⁡(d​λ+n​L2d​λ)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{\det V_{n}}{\lambda^{d}}\right)\leq d\log\left(\frac{d\lambda+nL^{2}}{d\lambda}\right) (71)

det(λ​I)=λd​ and ​Tr⁡(λ​I)=d​λ\displaystyle\det(\lambda I)=\lambda^{d}\text{ and }\Tr(\lambda I)=d\lambda (72)

detVn=∏iλi≤(1d​Tr⁡Vn)d≤(Tr⁡λ​I+n​L2d)d\displaystyle\det V_{n}=\prod_{i}\lambda_{i}\leq\left(\frac{1}{d}\Tr V_{n}\right)^{d}\leq\left(\frac{\Tr\lambda I+nL^{2}}{d}\right)^{d} (73)

because ‖ϕ‖≤L\left\lVert{\phi}\right\rVert\leq L. Thus we have

log⁡(detVnλd)≤d​log⁡(d​λ+n​L2d​λ)\displaystyle\log\left(\frac{\det V_{n}}{\lambda^{d}}\right)\leq d\log\left(\frac{d\lambda+nL^{2}}{d\lambda}\right) (74)

∎

A.5.2 Elliptical Potential Lemma

We here state a standard result, commonly referred to as the elliptical potential lemma, for completeness.

Lemma 1.

Assume V0≻0V_{0}\succ 0 be positive definite and let ϕ1,…,ϕn\phi_{1},\dots,\phi_{n} be a sequence of vectors with ‖ϕt‖≤L\left\lVert{\phi_{t}}\right\rVert\leq L for all t=1,…,nt=1,\dots,n, and Vt=V0+∑s=1tϕs​ϕs⊤V_{t}=V_{0}+\sum_{s=1}^{t}\phi_{s}\phi_{s}^{\top}.

∑t=1nmin⁡{1,‖ϕi‖Vt−1−12}≤2​log⁡(detVndetV0)\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{n}\min\{1,\left\lVert{\phi_{i}}\right\rVert^{2}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\}\leq 2\log\left(\frac{\det V_{n}}{\det V_{0}}\right) (75)
Proof.

First, note that we have for u≥0u\geq 0

min⁡{1,u}≤2​log⁡(1+u)\displaystyle\min\{1,u\}\leq 2\log(1+u) (76)

and use it to get

∑t=1nmin⁡{1,‖ϕt‖Vt−1−12}≤2​∑t=1nlog⁡(1+‖ϕt‖Vt−1−12)\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{n}\min\{1,\left\lVert{\phi_{t}}\right\rVert^{2}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\}\leq 2\sum_{t=1}^{n}\log\left(1+\left\lVert{\phi_{t}}\right\rVert^{2}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\right) (77)

Then, notice that for t≥1t\geq 1 we have

Vt=Vt−1+ϕtϕt⊤=Vt−11/2(I+Vt−1−1/2ϕtϕt⊤Vt−1−1/2)Vt−11/2\displaystyle V_{t}=V_{t-1}+\phi_{t}\phi_{t}^{\top}=V_{t-1}^{1/2}\left(I+V_{t-1}^{-1/2}\phi_{t}\phi_{t}^{\top}V_{t-1}^{-1/2}\right)V_{t-1}^{1/2} (78)

so, taking the determinant on both sides we get

detVt=detVt−1⋅det(I+Vt−1−1/2ϕtϕt⊤Vt−1−1/2)=detVt−1(1+‖ϕt‖Vt−1−12)\displaystyle\det V_{t}=\det V_{t-1}\cdot\det\left(I+V_{t-1}^{-1/2}\phi_{t}\phi_{t}^{\top}V_{t-1}^{-1/2}\right)=\det V_{t-1}\left(1+\left\lVert{\phi_{t}}\right\rVert^{2}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\right) (79)

where we used det(A+B)=detA⋅detB\det(A+B)=\det A\cdot\det B and det(I+u​u⊤)=1+‖u‖2\det(I+uu^{\top})=1+\left\lVert{u}\right\rVert^{2}. Telescoping the previous result, we get

detVn=detV0⋅∏t=1n(1+‖ϕt‖Vt−1−12)\displaystyle\det V_{n}=\det V_{0}\cdot\prod_{t=1}^{n}\left(1+\left\lVert{\phi_{t}}\right\rVert^{2}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\right) (80)

which implies

∑t=1nlog⁡(1+‖ϕt‖Vt−1−12)=log⁡(detVndetV0)\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^{n}\log\left(1+\left\lVert{\phi_{t}}\right\rVert^{2}_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}\right)=\log\left(\frac{\det V_{n}}{\det V_{0}}\right) (81)

which proves the claim. ∎

A.5.3 UCB Optimisation

We here state the derivation of a well-known property of LinUCB for completeness.

Remark 1.

We want to show that

arg​maxz∈𝒞t⁡maxw∈𝒞t​w⊤​ψ​(st,z)=arg​maxz∈𝒞t⁡ψ​(st,z)⊤​z^t−1+βt​‖ψ⁡(st,z)‖Vt−1−1\displaystyle\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\max_{w\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\,w^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z)=\argmax_{z\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}\,\psi(s_{t},z)^{\top}\hat{z}_{t-1}+\beta_{t}\left\lVert{\psi(s_{t},z)}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}^{-1}} (82)

Focusing on the inner max\max term, we have

maxw∈𝒞t⁡w⊤​ψ​(st,z)\displaystyle\max_{w\in\mathcal{C}_{t}}w^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z) =max‖w−z^t‖Vt−1≤βt⁡w⊤​ψ​(st,z)\displaystyle=\max_{\left\lVert{w-\hat{z}_{t}}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}}\leq\beta_{t}}w^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z) (83)
=z^t⊤​x+max‖u‖Vt−1≤βt⁡u⊤​ψ​(st,z)\displaystyle=\hat{z}_{t}^{\top}x+\max_{\left\lVert{u}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}}\leq\beta_{t}}u^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z) (84)
≤z^t⊤​ψ​(st,z)+max‖u‖Vt−1≤βt⁡‖u‖Vt−1​‖ψ⁡(st,z)‖Vt−1−1\displaystyle\leq\hat{z}_{t}^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z)+\max_{\left\lVert{u}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}}\leq\beta_{t}}\left\lVert{u}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}}\left\lVert{\psi(s_{t},z)}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}^{-1}} (85)
=z^t⊤​ψ​(st,z)+βt​‖ψ⁡(st,z)‖Vt−1−1\displaystyle=\hat{z}_{t}^{\top}\psi(s_{t},z)+\beta_{t}\left\lVert{\psi(s_{t},z)}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}^{-1}} (86)

where the equality is attained by

u⋆=βt​Vt−1−1​ψ​(st,z)‖ψ⁡(st,z)‖Vt−1−1\displaystyle u^{\star}=\beta_{t}\frac{V_{t-1}^{-1}\psi(s_{t},z)}{\left\lVert{\psi(s_{t},z)}\right\rVert_{V_{t-1}^{-1}}} (87)

Appendix B Additional Experiments

B.1 How much compute does OpTI-BFM need?

To estimate the compute cost of OpTI-BFM, we measure the time for the action selection and update steps on an Nvidia RTX 4090, skipping the first few calls to avoid measuring JIT compilation time. Table 1 shows that OpTI-BFM and OpTI-BFM-TS are about 5x and 4x slower than running just the policy (Oracle) respectively.

B.2 Requesting Reward Labels Explicitly

We have so far assumed that each environment interaction provides a reward label, and is thus synonymous with the labeling cost. One could also consider a setting where the agent can decide whether it wants to observe the reward label in each transition. A very simple approach in this setting is to threshold the D-gap (Kiefer & Wolfowitz, 1960; Lattimore & Szepesvári, 2020), which describes how much the confidence ellipsoid shrinks for a new ϕt\phi_{t}.

Δ(ϕt)=logdet(Vt−1+ϕtϕt⊤)−logdetVt−1=log(1+‖ϕt‖Vt−1−12)\displaystyle\Delta(\phi_{t})=\log\det(V_{t-1}+\phi_{t}\phi_{t}^{\top})-\log\det V_{t-1}=\log\left(1+\left\lVert{\phi_{t}}\right\rVert^{2}_{V^{-1}_{t-1}}\right) (88)

This approach can be directly applied to OpTI-BFM by introducing a hyper-parameter κ\kappa and only requesting rtr_{t} if Δ⁡(ϕt)≥κ\Delta(\phi_{t})\geq\kappa. We evaluate labeling efficiency for this variant: for each labeling budget nn (# Samples), we measure average rewards at the time step tt in which the budget is exhausted, i.e. 1t​∑i=1trt\tfrac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}r_{t}. This is presented in Fig. 7 (see also Fig. 12 and Fig. 13 for per-task results). We observe that κ\kappa trades-off environment interaction and labeling cost: for higher κ\kappa, good performance is achieved with fewer labels, but more episodes are required to request the same number of labels. Given a specific cost for labels, a slightly more involved thresholding scheme (Tucker et al., 2023) could potentially be used to decide the threshold apriori. Surprisingly, this variant of OpTI-BFM can maintain the performance of the main algorithm, especially in easier tasks, while reducing the amount of labeled data by one order of magnitude.

Appendix C Full Experimental Results

Appendix D Training Protocol

D.1 Forward Backward Framework

We use the forward backward (FB) framework (Touati & Ollivier, 2021) as the base BFM throught our experiments. To fully explain FB, we quickly introduce the successor measure (Dayan, 1993; Blier et al., 2021) MπM^{\pi}; it is defined as

Mπ(s0,a0,X)=∑t≥0γtPr[st∈X|s0,a0,π].\displaystyle M^{\pi}(s_{0},a_{0},X)=\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\Pr[s_{t}\in X|s_{0},a_{0},\pi]. (89)

and can be thought of as the discounted state occupancy of a policy π\pi when starting in s0,a0s_{0},a_{0}. FB then learns the low-rank decomposition of the successor measure density w.r.t. the empirical dataset measure 𝒟train​(d​s)\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}(ds):

Mπz​(s,a,d​s+)=F​(s,a,z)⊤​B​(s+)​𝒟train​(d​s+).\displaystyle M^{\pi_{z}}(s,a,ds^{+})=F(s,a,z)^{\top}B(s^{+})\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}(ds^{+}). (90)

where the policy should satisfy

πz​(a|s)>0⟹a∈arg​maxa⁡F​(s,a,z)⊤​z.\displaystyle\pi_{z}(a|s)>0\implies a\in\argmax_{a}F(s,a,z)^{\top}z. (91)

The successor measure and successor features are closely related, since we have that

ψπ​(s,a)=∫Mπ​(s,a,d​s+)​ϕ​(s+).\displaystyle\psi^{\pi}(s,a)=\int M^{\pi}(s,a,ds^{+})\phi(s^{+}). (92)

Following Touati & Ollivier (2021) (Theorem 13), we thus have for FB

∫B⁡(s+)​Mzπ​(s,a,d​s+)\displaystyle\int B(s^{+})M^{\pi}_{z}(s,a,ds^{+}) =∫B⁡(s+)​B​(s+)⊤​𝒟train​(d​s+)​F​(s,a,z)\displaystyle=\int B(s^{+})B(s^{+})^{\top}\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}(ds^{+})F(s,a,z) (93)
=𝔼s∼𝒟train​[B⁡(s+)​B​(s+)⊤]​F​(s,a,z)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}[B(s^{+})B(s^{+})^{\top}]F(s,a,z) (94)
=(Cov𝒟train​B)​F​(s,a,z)\displaystyle=(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B)F(s,a,z) (95)

so F⁡(s,a,z)F(s,a,z) are SFs of features ϕ⁡(s)=(Cov𝒟train​B)−1​B​(s)\phi(s)=(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B)^{-1}B(s). Task inference for FB with labeled dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} then effectively becomes

zr\displaystyle z_{r} =(Cov𝒟​ϕ)−1​𝔼​[ϕ⁡(s)​r​(s)]\displaystyle=(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}}\phi)^{-1}\mathbb{E}[\phi(s)r(s)] (96)
=(Cov𝒟​((Cov𝒟train​B)−1​B))−1​(Cov𝒟train​B)−1​𝔼​[B⁡(s)​r​(s)]\displaystyle=\left(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}}\left((\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B)^{-1}B\right)\right)^{-1}(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B)^{-1}\mathbb{E}[B(s)r(s)] (97)
=(Cov𝒟train​B)​(Cov𝒟​B)−1​(Cov𝒟train​B)​(Cov𝒟train​B)−1​𝔼​[B⁡(s)​r​(s)]\displaystyle=(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B)(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}}B)^{-1}(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B)(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B)^{-1}\mathbb{E}[B(s)r(s)] (98)
=(Cov𝒟train​B)​(Cov𝒟​B)−1​𝔼​[B⁡(s)​r​(s)]\displaystyle=(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B)(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}}B)^{-1}\mathbb{E}[B(s)r(s)] (99)

which is consistent with Touati & Ollivier (2021) (Proposition 15). In practice we pre-compute (Cov𝒟train​B)(\mathrm{Cov}_{\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}B) with 50k samples from 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} after training.

D.2 Pre-training

As is the standard in zero-shot RL benchmarks (Touati et al., 2023; Agarwal et al., 2025b), we train our FB model using an offline dataset collected with RND (Burda et al., 2018; Yarats et al., 2022) consisting of 10M transitions.

FB is trained using 3 losses. Firstly, the successor measure loss (Blier et al., 2021)

ℒF​B(z)=𝔼s,a,s′∼𝒟traina′∼πz(⋅|s′)𝔼s+∼𝒟train[\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{FB}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s,a,s^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\\ a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{z}(\cdot|s^{\prime})\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}_{s^{+}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}\bigg[ −2​F​(s,a,z)⊤​B​(s′)\displaystyle-2F(s,a,z)^{\top}B(s^{\prime}) (100)
+(F(s,a,z)⊤B(s+)−γF¯(s′,a′,z)⊤B¯(s+))2],\displaystyle+\left(F(s,a,z)^{\top}B(s^{+})-\gamma\overline{F}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},z)^{\top}\overline{B}(s^{+})\right)^{2}\bigg], (101)

where F¯,B¯\overline{F},\overline{B} are target networks, secondly, an orthogonality regularizing loss on BB

ℒortho=𝔼s∼𝒟trains′∼𝒟train​[−2​‖B⁡(s)‖22+B​(s)⊤​B​(s′)],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{ortho}}=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}s\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\\ s^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}\end{subarray}}\left[-2\left\lVert{B(s)}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}+B(s)^{\top}B(s^{\prime})\right], (102)

and thirdly a DDPG-style loss for π\pi:

ℒπ(z)=𝔼s∼𝒟train𝔼a∼πz(⋅|s)[−F(s,a,z)⊤z],\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\pi}(z)=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{z}(\cdot|s)}\left[-F(s,a,z)^{\top}z\right], (103)

using the reparameterization trick for Gaussian policies.

D.3 Architecture and Hyper-parameters

We choose to follow the implementation details of the most recent work on FB (Tirinzoni et al., 2025), specifically their implementation for DMC in the released code-base. The BB-network is a 3-layer MLP. The FF is an ensemble of size 2 with each two 2-layer MLPs to encode the arguments (s,a)(s,a) and (s,z)(s,z) that are then concatenated and fed into another 2-layer MLP. π\pi uses two 2-layer MLPs to encode the arguments ss and (s,z)(s,z) and then also another 2-layer MLP to map from the concatenated layers to a mean μ\mu. The policy is then a truncated Gaussian with fixed standard deviation of σ=0.2\sigma=0.2 that truncates at 1.5​σ1.5\sigma. The rest of the pre-training hyper-parameters are listed in Table 2 below. The task embedding space of FB is the dd-dimensional hyper-sphere since the optimal policy πz\pi_{z} is invariant to the scale of the reward function. Note that OpTI-BFM cannot make this simplification because it tries to estimate the hidden parameter of the reward function and not the latent that is plugged into the policy. We can recover the latter easily with an L2 normalization.

Appendix E Experiment Protocol

We evaluate our methods on a common zero-shot RL benchmark (Touati et al., 2023; Agarwal et al., 2025b). The benchmark consists of the Walker, Cheetah, and Quadruped environments from DMC (Tassa et al., 2018) with four tasks (reward functions) each. Note that each task has randomized initial states, so when evaluating single episode performance, e.g. Fig. 9, we report the mean over 20 episodes. And when evaluating task inference performance over multiple episode, e.g., Figs. 2 and 10, we report the mean over 10 trials. All error-bars and shaded regions denote min-max-intervals over three training seeds around mean performance.

E.1 Custom Walker Velocity Tasks

The custom tasks we implement for DMC Walker Fig. 5 consist of only the velocity tracking components of the stand, walk, and run tasks. Further note that, by default, higher velocity is always allowed: a running policy will also perform rather well in standing. For this reason, we modify the velocity reward bonus so that it is 1 if the velocity matches the target exactly, and then linearly tapers to 0.5 when off by 2. From there, the reward then directly drops to 0.

Appendix F Inference Hyper-Parameters

For each experiment and method we perform a grid-search over hyper-parameters. We then choose the hyper-parameters with highest overall cumulative return per environment for each method to report performance.

F.1 OpTI-BFM

We found both OpTI-BFM and OpTI-BFM-TS to be very robust to the hyper-parameters we tested. For each method we consider a single hyper-parameter with three values each: For UCB, we test a fixed βt=β∈{1.0,0.1,0.001}\beta_{t}=\beta\in\{1.0,0.1,0.001\}. For TS, we test σ∈{0.1,0.001,0.0001}\sigma\in\{0.1,0.001,0.0001\}. This means all other parameters where held constant. Specifically, ρ=1\rho=1 and λ=1\lambda=1 if not reported otherwise (Fig. 5). The number of samples for the UCB optimization was n=128n=128 throughout all experiments.

F.2 LoLA

For LoLA we consider a range of hyper-parameters to trade-off exploration, update frequency, update step-size, and variance in the gradient. We search all combinations of:

  • •

    horizon length and task embedding update rate {50,100,250}\{50,100,250\} as in Sikchi et al. (2025);

  • •

    learning rate {0.1,0.05}\{0.1,0.05\} as in Sikchi et al. (2025);

  • •

    standard deviation of the Gaussian on the task embedding {0.05,0.1,0.2}\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}.

  • •

    The batch size reported in Sikchi et al. (2025) is 5-10: we thus consider a replay buffer of 1000, which results in an effective batch size of 20, 10, and 4 for the respective update rates.
